title: Stop Robocalls on the Home Phone: Landline Call Blockers and Scam-Blocking Cordless Phones
subtitle: Two ways to quiet a ringing landline, with no apps to learn, plus what they can and cannot stop.
excerpt: If Mom or Dad still answers the home phone, a plug-in call blocker or a cordless phone with built-in call blocking may cut down on robocalls. Here is how each works and what to check before you buy.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: For many families, the home phone is still the line that matters. Every ring can mean getting up from a comfortable chair, only to hear a recording or a stranger with a story.

Two kinds of gadgets are made for this problem: a small call blocker that connects to your home phone line, and a cordless phone with call blocking built in. One thing to know up front: both only work on a home phone line. They do not protect a cell phone or text messages, and they are not a fit for anyone who mostly uses a cell phone.

CPR Call Blockers makes a plug-in blocker. The maker says setup is plugging it into the home phone line, and that a large one-touch BLOCK NOW button blocks a new caller. The maker also says there are no apps, no Wi-Fi (no wireless internet) and no subscription. The CPR V5000 listing at Verizon says it blocks unwanted robocalls, stores 5000 numbers in memory and lets you add 1500 numbers of your own.

A scam-blocking cordless phone does the job inside the phone itself, so there is no extra box. Panasonic says its Automated Call Block pre-blocks robocalls by prompting callers to press 1 to connect. Its Telemarketing Call Block blocks announced callers. The phone also shows a confirmation screen before you return a one-ring call, and its talking Caller ID announces the caller in English or Spanish.
"Talk to people, not computers." — Panasonic, KX-TGD83x product page

It is worth being honest about the limits. Because Automated Call Block depends on callers pressing 1, a live scammer may still get through. Panasonic's list of 1,000 extra blocked numbers will not stop spoofed numbers (fake caller ID) that keep changing. Automated calls you want, such as a pharmacy or school alert, might be blocked unless you add them to the phone's allow list.

items: Check what kind of phone service you have first. CPR's Verizon listing mentions Fios, and it does not say whether the V5000 works with VoIP (phone service over the internet) or digital phone lines. If you have cable or internet phone service, check with the maker before you buy.

Look at the true cost. The Panasonic is a plain phone with no monthly fee. CPR says on its homepage there is no subscription, and the Verizon page states no monthly fee. Prices can vary by seller, so check the current price.
Find a big, clearly marked block button. CPR's BLOCK NOW button is meant to block a new caller, and Panasonic has a 1-touch Call Block button for its extra 1,000 numbers.
For a phone, check the screen and sound. Panasonic lists a large white backlit display, a backlit keypad, and talking Caller ID, which can help if eyesight is not what it was.
Know the return policy. CPR's own website lists a 30-day money-back guarantee and free shipping; if you buy from another store, check that store's policy.
Ask whether important callers can be allowed through, such as the pharmacy or a school. Panasonic mentions an allow list.
For a cordless phone, check battery life and handsets. Panasonic lists up to 10 hours of talk time and 5 days of standby in eco mode, and the system expands to 6 handsets.

sections.content: Setting It Up and Using It Well

For a CPR blocker, follow the maker's instructions for plugging it into the home phone line. If you have any doubt about your type of phone service, ask the maker first. The 30-day return window on CPR's site gives some room to try it.

With the Panasonic phone, extra handsets can go in the bedroom or kitchen if that saves steps. Then sit down together and think about which numbers must always get through, such as family, doctors, the pharmacy and any service that sends automated reminders, and check how to add them to the phone's allow list.
The Panasonic phone can also record calls, and it announces "Start Recording" at the start of the call. Rules about recording phone calls vary by state, so check yours before relying on that feature.
No blocker catches every call. The one rule that always applies: never give money, passwords or codes to someone who calls out of the blue.
sections.label: Good to Know

sections.content: A quieter phone can make a real difference in a parent's day. Pick the one that fits the phone service in the house, check the current price, and keep that one rule handy by the phone.
